rules: The model selects topic IDs only. Domains and groups are derived from topic placements by code; the model never names a domain.
Select every topic the record substantively covers, and none that it merely mentions. Zero topics is valid; keep the record and use unmapped_concepts.
A topic may sit in several domains (placements). A record therefore appears in several domain views but is counted once overall. Domain counts overlap and must not be added together.
The first placement is the topic's home domain, and the ID prefix matches the home domain's prefix.
An ID is never reused for a different meaning. A retired or moved ID is listed in legacy_ids of its successor(s). A topic carved out of a topic that still exists lists it in split_from.
Use a sector topic for a sector measure (flood defences = WAT-03). Use a Disaster Risk Management topic only when the subject is the cross-sector disaster-risk system itself.
Membership of the Climate domain does not establish climate causation; an earthquake is never climate evidence.

domains.label: Agriculture & Food

domains.label: Water
domains.definition: Water resources, supply, basins, drought, floods and coasts, water quality and the cryosphere as a water source.

domains.label: Nature, Forests & Land

domains.label: Energy
domains.definition: Energy supply, renewables, grids, efficiency, heating, fossil-fuel transition and methane.

domains.label: Settlements & Infrastructure

domains.label: Transport

domains.label: Industry & Mining
domains.definition: Industrial production, processes, industrial resilience, mining and extractives.

domains.label: Health

domains.label: Waste & Circular Economy
domains.definition: Materials and recycling, solid waste and landfill methane, wastewater.

domains.label: Economy & Transition

domains.label: Livelihoods & Social Protection

domains.label: Culture & Heritage

rules: Only extract labels explicitly supported by the record's own evidence.
One primary topic; secondary topics only for substantive additional subjects.
Empty arrays mean not stated or not extracted, never that the concept does not exist.
Unknown labels go in unmapped_concepts with the source wording; never invent enum values.
No human review_status field. Automatic check states and post-publication user overlays are separate.
Do not reward a record for carrying more labels.
Delivery details require source-linked actor, action timeframe and specific verifiable deliverable for the same coherent response and variant. A broad programme name alone is not shared identity.
Only enabled facets are included in the routine extraction contract. Disabled vocabularies remain editable optional modules, not empty claims about the absence of those concepts.
priority_evidence is a nullable sourced field, not an importance label, ranking or scoring weight.

A null primary_topic_id means an unmapped subject. statement_type other means a sourced assertion for which no predefined statement type fits. Missing classification is not other. Preserve these independently; never move unmapped records into an invented Other domain.

options.meaning: A stated risk, vulnerability, impact, need, barrier or gap
A current or historical condition, capacity or baseline
A modeled or expected future condition, not a policy undertaking
An attributable policy goal, priority or target
A specific planned measure, programme or instrument
Explicit implementation, procurement, construction or operation of the identified action
Explicitly completed, installed or adopted output of the identified action
A reported outcome or effect; does not by itself prove causation or target achievement
A recommendation without an attributable adopted undertaking
Relevant sourced statement that no listed type fits

label_catalogue.relationship_rule: Equivalent restatements, explicit progress and revisions may connect assertions of the same identified proposition/intervention. A shared programme name or topic is insufficient identity. Supporting/context assertions retain their own identities and documentation bands. Supersession requires explicit evidence. Contradiction requires comparable scope and basis.

user_overlay.rule: Store reason, actor, timestamp and claim version separately. A flag does not stop publication. Hiding changes presentation only by default; a custom exclusion produces a labeled adjusted score, leaving the generated regional benchmark intact.

core.reason: The smallest useful set for routine regional climate and disaster policy filtering.

additional_context.reason: Enable for an explicit inclusion or thematic analysis question. Source statements and quotations remain available while structured tags are disabled; automatic structured coverage is not promised until retagging or re-extraction.

specialist_risk.reason: Specialist risk analysis beyond the ordinary topic/band dashboard.

priority_evidence.meaning: Exact source wording that explicitly calls this concern, need or response a priority; never inferred importance.

raw_shape.text: Exact priority wording from an allowed evidence quotation
raw_shape.evidence_refs: Non-empty list of local evidence references from this extraction response

normalized_shape.evidence_ids: Non-empty list of persistent evidence IDs mapped by code

priority_evidence.rule: A source may prioritize a risk or need without documenting a response. Repetition, hazard severity, document length and model judgement never create priority_evidence. Priority filtering does not change benchmark denominators or bands.

scoring.aggregation: Sum each distinct grouped claim once per topic, domain or country scope. Overlapping topic/domain rows must not be added together.
scoring.normalization: Standardized regional score = 100 * Phi((raw - regional mean) / population SD), where Phi is the standard normal cumulative distribution function. The regional mean maps to 50; -1/+1 SD to 15.9/84.1; -2/+2 SD to 2.3/97.7. At least two complete non-demo countries are required in the same country/domain/topic scope. Equal totals (zero SD), including all-zero totals, receive 50 by convention. Partial results are excluded. The reference uses the full eligible region, independent of display filters. This is a standardized score, not an observed percentile or percentage implementation. Colors use the same raw population SD.

pages.text:
2025
Nationally determined contribution
of the Republic of Kazakhstan to the
global response to climate change
until 2035

Foreword
The Republic of Kazakhstan remains firmly
committed to advancing a low-carbon,
climate-resilient future while safeguarding
the well-being of our people and the
sustainability of our economy.
As one of the world’s largest landlocked developing countries, Kazakhstan
faces distinct vulnerabilities, from water scarcity and extreme weather
events to the socioeconomic implications of transitioning from fossil fuels.
Yet, we remain determined to act with both honesty and ambition.
This Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0) reaffirms Kazakhstan’s
commitment under the Paris Agreement to contribute to global climate
action and reflects a higher level of ambition compared to the previous NDC.
It outlines our strengthened efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions,
enhance adaptation, and build resilience to climate impacts, while
also setting the foundation for achieving carbon neutrality by 2060, the
overarching goal that guides our national climate policy framework.
Kazakhstan continues to make tangible progress from advancing renewable
energy and modernizing district heating systems, to restoring ecosystems
and expanding climate-smart agriculture. We are mobilizing domestic
resources while calling for stronger international cooperation and support to
ensure a just and inclusive transition, and to enable the full realization of our
NDC 3.0 ambition.
Kazakhstan acts with determination and responsibility in fulfilling its
global commitments. Achieving carbon neutrality by 2060 will require
sustained effort, innovation, and partnership. With the continued support
of the international community, Kazakhstan stands ready to demonstrate
leadership and contribute to a sustainable and climate-resilient future for
generations to come.
Minister of Ecology and Natural Resources
Yerlan Nyssanbayev
2

Acknowledgement
The Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources of the Republic of
Kazakhstan expresses its sincere appreciation to all ministries, agencies,
and organizations that contributed to the preparation of the Nationally
Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0).
The Ministry gratefully acknowledges the support of international
development partners, including the Asian Development Bank (ADB),
Deutsche Gesellschaft für Internationale Zusammenarbeit (GIZ), the
Embassies of the Federal Republic of Germany and the United Kingdom,
the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), NDC
Partnership, the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF), the United
Nations Development Programme (UNDP), the United Nations Institute
for Training and Research (UNITAR), for their continuous assistance,
technical expertise, and commitment to advancing Kazakhstan’s climate
agenda.
The Ministry also recognizes the contributions of the Asian Disaster
Preparedness Center (ADPC), ECOJER Association, and the Stockholm

Summary
The Republic of Kazakhstan reaffirms its strong commitment to the
objectives of the Paris Agreement through the submission of its enhanced
Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0). Building upon previous
efforts, NDC 3.0 reflects a significant step-up in national ambition and
transparency, aligning Kazakhstan’s development trajectory with the
long-term goal of achieving carbon neutrality by 2060.
NDC 3.0 covers the common 2026–2035 time frame and is aligned with
the Strategy on Achieving Carbon Neutrality by 2060. It is backed by an
updated Environmental Code, a revitalized Emissions Trading System
(ETS), and programs on green finance, afforestation, energy efficiency,
renewable energy, and climate-resilient infrastructure, with a forthcoming
National Adaptation Plan and links to the National Development Plan to
2029.
The target covers all IPCC sectors and gases with emissions and removals
estimated by using IPCC 2006 Guidelines with AR5 GWPs.
Under the unconditional pathway, net emissions reach ~328 MtCO₂e in
2030 (15%) and ~320 MtCO₂e (17%) by 2035, driven by a cleaner power mix
that lifts the share of renewables and other low-emission sources toward
~35 percent by 2035; with international support, emissions can fall to
~288 MtCO₂e by 2035. The NDC integrates adaptation, loss and damage,
and a just transition.
7
The NDC raises Kazakhstan’s mitigation target, with national net
greenhouse gas emissions set to decline by 17 percent below
1990 levels by 2035 (unconditional) and up to 25 percent with
international support.
This NDC reflects Kazakhstan’s comprehensive, whole-
of-government approach to climate policy, supported by
strong inter-ministerial coordination and the engagement
of civil society, private sector, and international partners.
It operationalizes national climate strategies, including
the Strategy on Achieving Carbon Neutrality by 2060 and
the Action Plan for the Transition to a Green Economy, by
translating long-term goals into measurable sectoral targets
and investment priorities.

Progress will be tracked against the most recent reported 1990 net emissions
in the Biennial Transparency Report, with any recalculations being applied
in line with IPCC good-practice guidance. The document was prepared
through an inclusive process involving ministries, sub-national authorities,
experts, civil society, the private sector, and international partners.
Kazakhstan recognizes that achieving these targets requires sustained
domestic effort and enhanced international cooperation.
The country continues to mobilize national resources while calling for
predictable, concessional, and technology-oriented international support
to enable deeper decarbonization, accelerate adaptation, and ensure a
just and equitable transition.
Through NDC 3.0, Kazakhstan demonstrates its determination to
contribute meaningfully to the global effort to limit temperature increase,
while ensuring sustainable development and the well-being of present
and future generations.
Implementation is underpinned by market and transparency systems,
strengthening the ETS with tighter carbon budgets and improved
MRV, and enabling participation in Article 6 with clear authorizations,
corresponding adjustments, safeguards, and required institutions and
systems, while prioritizing just transition and inclusion.
The new NDC of Kazakhstan is all about growth through innovation and
modernization and best use of talents of people and natural resource
endowment, and not about scarcity and constrains.
8
Indicative investment needs for 2026–2035 are estimated at about
USD 175,6 billion (USD 128.5 billion for mitigation; USD 47 billion for
adaptation), or roughly 5.5 percent of current GDP annually; counting
only additional costs above BAU, needs are ~USD 71.8 billion (~2.5
percent of GDP annually). Kazakhstan estimates requirements for
around USD 20 billion in highly concessional international finance.
Kazakhstan has already financed a large share of climate action
domestically through the republican budget, SOEs, and local
delivery systems.

Introduction
The Paris Agreement, adopted in 2015, set the global course for limiting
temperature rise to well below 2 °C and pursuing efforts to keep it to
1.5 °C, while strengthening adaptive capacity and aligning finance with
low-emission, climate-resilient development pathways.
Determined Contributions (NDCs) are the core instruments for achieving
these goals and are updated every five years to reflect increasing ambition,
in line with countries’ circumstances and the principle of common but
differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities.
The first Global Stocktake (GST), concluded at COP28, provided a
comprehensive assessment of collective progress under the Paris
Agreement. It underscored the urgency of deep, rapid and sustained
reductions in GHG emissions in line with 1.5 °C pathways, strengthening
adaptation, and scaling up support for developing economies.
The GST also strengthened calls for transitioning away from fossil fuels in
the energy systems, with a particular focus on accelerating efforts towards
the phase-down of unabated coal-based electricity and deploying clean
energy alternatives in line with national circumstances. It emphasized the
importance of conserving, protecting and restoring nature and ecosystems
towards achieving the Paris Agreement temperature goal. With regards
to adaptation, the GST called for significantly scaling up adaptation efforts,
including doubling adaptation finance by 2025, enhancing national
planning and implementation, and acknowledged the role of the Global
Goal on Adaptation (GGA) to guide countries’ adaptation effort towards
enhancing resilience, especially in vulnerable sectors and regions.
In 2023, the Government adopted the Strategy on Achieving Carbon
Neutrality by 2060, signaling a decisive long-term transition toward a
diversified, low-emission economy.
This strategy is supported by a strengthened Environmental Code, a
revitalized Emissions Trading System, and programs on green finance,
afforestation, energy efficiency, renewable energy deployment, and
climate-resilient infrastructure.

Kazakhstan’s NDC 3.0 responds to this global call by enhancing

1.1. National Circumstances
Kazakhstan is the world’s largest landlocked country and an LLDC. Its
vast territory, continental climate, and distance to seaports shape logistics
costs, energy security, and adaptation needs. Major river systems are
transboundary, which makes water availability and allocation a strategic
concern for agriculture, industry, and cities. Regional development
is uneven, with coal- and mining-dependent oblasts facing distinct
transition challenges.
The economy is diversified yet energy and materials intensive. Heavy
industry, mining and metals, oil and gas, and transport are major
contributors to GDP, exports, and employment.
12
With its NDC 3.0 submission, Kazakhstan raises its mitigation
ambition in line with its national circumstances and long-
term Strategy on Achieving Carbon Neutrality by 2060,
demonstrating commitment to the collective effort and
charting a credible pathway to contribute fairly to the global
goal of limiting temperature rise while building a resilient,
inclusive, and sustainable economy at home.
The country’s NDC 3.0 also gives particular attention to a just
transition for coal-dependent regions, to sustainable water and land
management, to climate-smart agriculture, and to the protection
of vulnerable groups, including women, youth, children, rural and
low-income communities, thereby embedding the principles of
inclusivity and fairness into Kazakhstan’s climate agenda.

Power generation relies significantly on coal, with gas and hydropower
providing balancing roles. Grid reliability, aging assets, and winter
peak constraints influence the pace and sequencing of clean energy
integration.
Floods and droughts already threaten lives and livelihoods in Kazakhstan,
and climate change is intensifying and shifting these hazards.
As the impacts of climate change deepen, patterns of drought and
flooding are likely to change. While formal event attribution for floods in
Kazakhstan is still developing, the Government treats flood and drought
risk as a primary concern for climate change adaptation, disaster risk
reduction, and long-term socio-economic development. Kazakhstan will
plan and invest on the basis that climate change is already altering hazard
patterns, while continuing to refine attribution with new data.
Kazakhstan’s GHG profile reflects its economic structure. While per capita
emissions remain higher than the global average (about 14t CO₂-eq in
2023 due to its historic reliance on coal and energy-intensive industries),
the country’s overall contribution to global emissions is less than 0.7
percent. This imbalance, with mounting climate-related losses despite
a relatively small share in global emissions, underscores the urgency of
pursuing a low-emission, climate-resilient development pathway.

1.3. Challenges in implementing the NDC
The continental climate drives very high winter heating demand and rising
summer cooling demand. Conventional air-source heat pumps perform
poorly at sub-zero temperatures. Sustainable biomass potential is limited
and undeveloped, while expanding domestic natural-gas development is
capital-intensive slow.
Hydropower is constrained by variable and declining inflows on
transboundary rivers influenced by upstream withdrawals and climate-
driven glacial retreat.
Coal therefore remains an important, though carbon-intensive, source
of heat and power in the near term. Energy planning also underweights
adaptation needs such as peak loads during heatwaves and higher
electricity demand for irrigation and cooling.
Although the government is prioritizing renewables and gasification,
energy planning often overlooks adaptation needs such as rising cooling
and irrigation demand, as well as power-system vulnerability to peak
loads during heatwaves.
Socio-economic dependence on coal is significant on several oblasts. Jobs,
local budgets and supply chains are tied to coal mining and coal-based
power. A just transition framework is nascent, and practical guidance for
reskilling workers, diversifying local economies, and protecting affected
households remain limited.
Carbon pricing reforms are essential for decarbonization but could raise
energy and transport costs if not carefully sequenced and paired with
targeted social protection.
Financial conditions remain a significant obstacle. Green
investments face high capital costs compared to fossil fuel-
based projects due to low end-user tariffs, persistent fossil
fuel subsidies, and limited access to affordable long-term
financing. Innovative equipment is often not accepted as
collateral, limiting borrowing options.

with adaptation, pair technical and ecosystem-based solutions, and
strengthen institutional and human capacity at national and sub-national

2.1. Policies related to mitigation
Over the past decade, Kazakhstan has built a more coherent policy
and legislative framework to guide the low-carbon transition and align
national development with global climate objectives.
This framework combines long-term strategies, medium-term
development plans, regulatory reforms and market-based instruments,
providing a foundation for achieving the targets set in the NDC 3.0 and
the national goal of carbon neutrality by 2060.
Kazakhstan’s long-term climate policy is guided by the Strategy on
Achieving Carbon Neutrality by 2060, adopted in 2023.
The Strategy defines the national decarbonisation trajectory, outlining
sectoral pathways and investment needs estimated at USD 610 billion
to 2060. It calls for redirecting existing capital flows toward green
technologies and mobilising new public and private investment.
A detailed Roadmap is being developed to guide implementation and
sectoral sequencing.
The National Development Plan to 2029 (adopted 2024) establishes
priorities for 2025–2029, promoting diversification, innovation, and
human-capital development as enablers of a just, low-emission transition.
The Action Plan for Transition to a Green Economy (2024–2030)
complements this by setting concrete green-finance and sustainable-
investment targets, including increased issuance of green loans and
bonds by 2030.
Together, these plans connect Kazakhstan’s long-term carbon-neutral
vision with near-term policy and investment priorities.

2.2. National GHG Emissions (1990–2023)
Kazakhstan’s greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions have undergone marked
shifts since 1990, reflecting the country’s profound economic transitions
and structural changes in the energy system. In 1990, during the final years
of the Soviet-era industrial economy, net GHG emissions stood at about
385 Mt CO₂-equivalent, driven by energy-intensive heavy industry and a
strong reliance on fossil fuels. After a rapid decline in the 1990s, emissions
stabilized and then began to grow again in the early 2000s. According to
the most recent national inventory, net emissions reached about
349.2 Mt CO₂-equivalent in 2023.
24
Recently, Kazakhstan’s total GHG emissions rose in
2023 compared to 2021, driven by post-COVID economic
recovery and increased energy use.
However, total net emissions in 2023 remained 9.4% below 1990 levels.
The energy sector remains the dominant source of
emissions, contributing 79.8% (278.5 MtCO₂e) of the total
in 2023, with energy industries alone accounting for
about 40 % of national net emissions.

2.5. Measures to mitigate GHG emissions
Kazakhstan’s NDC 3.0 mitigation strategy is built around a package of
priority unconditional measures across all major emitting sectors. These
measures are designed to accelerate the country’s energy transition,
strengthen energy efficiency, promote low-emission technologies in
transport, industry and agriculture, scale up nature-based solutions and
improve waste management. In addition, the mitigation strategy places

Furthermore, institutional and legal regulation of methane will be

with the European Union Methane Regulation and the Global Methane

NDCs will also reduce short-lived climate pollutants (SLCPs). Modernizing
the thermal power industry and switching to cleaner fuels will reduce
emissions of black carbon and particulate matter.
Expanding energy efficiency programs and developing public
transportation will reduce urban air pollution. Implementing methane
capture and use systems at industrial facilities, landfills, and in agriculture
will reduce emissions of methane—the most significant SLCP. At the same
time, waste management measures and improved manure management
will reduce both methane and nitrous oxide.
Taken together, these measures will not only contribute to achieving
climate goals but also deliver tangible social and environmental benefits,
including improved air quality, public health, and resilience to climate
risks.
2.6. Socio-economic considerations
Kazakhstan will manage the social and economic implications of
decarbonization, so mitigation is feasible, fair, and investable. The
Government will protect vulnerable groups, support workers and regions
in transition, and expand participation and opportunity as new sectors
grow.
Kazakhstan’s transition to a low-emission economy will require gradual
decline in coal and other fossil fuels, especially in power generation and
heating. This transition brings important social and economic challenges
for coal-dependent regions, where local budgets, jobs and infrastructure
have long relied on the coal industry. To ensure that no region or
community is left behind, the Government will pursue a just transition
that:
• assessing local labour markets and skills,
• supporting re-training and re-deployment of workers,
• diversifying regional economies, and
• providing social protection for affected households.
36
A just and inclusive transition

Women and men experience climate risks and the transition differently
due to unequal access to resources, land, finance, and decision-making.
Women play central roles in household energy, water management, and
small-scale farming, making them indispensable partners in the shift to
low-emission and climate-resilient practices.
Kazakhstan has made progress by embedding gender considerations
into national policies and launching initiatives such as the Women for
Just Transition Network.
Gender-responsive climate policy will not only make mitigation more
effective but also promote fairer distribution of opportunities and
benefits.
Children and youth are both vulnerable to climate risks and key agents of
change in the transformation toward a green economy.

3.1. Kazakhstan’s efforts and achievements
in climate change adaptation
3.1.1. Adaptation related policies and plans
Kazakhstan’s adaptation policy is shaped by a comprehensive legal and
strategic f ramework that integrates climate risk considerations into
national development and sectoral planning.
The Environmental Code (2021) mandates systematic vulnerability
assessments, sectoral adaptation plans, prioritizing water management,
agriculture, forestry, and emergency preparedness.
The Water Code (2025) includes a separate chapter dedicated to
adaptation issues, which provides for the integration of climate risks
into water resources management and planning. The Code establishes
principles for assessing the impact of climate change on water
resources, ensuring the sustainable use of surface and groundwater, and
prioritizing water supply to critical sectors during periods of water scarcity.
The Concept of Transition to a Green Economy (2013, updated 2024)
expands ecosystem-based approaches, restoration of degraded land, and
sustainable water and soil management.
These policies provide a foundation but also reveal where integration
across sectors is still limited.
40
Sectoral strategies translate these policies and plans
into concrete action:
The Comprehensive plan for the development of the water
sector for 2024–2028 (2024) prioritizes efficiency, modern
irrigation, and infrastructure resilience.
The Concept for the Development of the Agro-Industrial
Complex for 2021-2030 (2021) promotes climate-smart farming
and water-saving crops.

3.1.2. Adaptation measures and current efforts
Kazakhstan’s adaptation actions focus largely on technical and
inf rastructure-driven measures, especially in water, agriculture, and
disaster risk reduction. These include, among others:
• Reinforcing flood and mudflow protection, de-risking moraine lakes,
and expanding early-warning and monitoring systems (Ministry of
Emergency Situations, 2023).
• Development and implementation of unified national rules for all
regions on population evacuation (routes, transport, temporary
accommodation) and protection of critical inf rastructure facilities
(energy, water supply, transport) in the context of climate-induced
emergencies (Ministry for Emergency Situations, 2023).
• Expansion of the hydrological monitoring network on small and
medium-sized rivers to improve the accuracy of flood forecasting and
enhance modelling systems (Ministry for Emergency Situations).
• Development and deployment of digital systems and specialized
software for modelling and forecasting the consequences of climate-
induced emergencies, with subsequent integration into the national
risk management system (Ministry for Emergency Situations).
• Equipping civil protection units with modern monitoring and response
tools, including unmanned aerial vehicles, satellite observation
systems, and mobile early-warning complexes (Ministry for Emergency
Situations).
• Advancing digitalized epidemiological surveillance and creating
a national forecasting and biosafety system by 2026 (Ministry of
Healthcare, 2022).
41
Increasing water storage capacity to 2.65 billion m³ by 2028,
reducing irrigation losses from 50 % to 35 %, modernizing canals, and
strengthening hydrological monitoring (Ministry of Water Resources
and Irrigation, 2024).
Scaling up climate-smart agriculture, diversifying away from water-
intensive crops, promoting organic farming, and restoring 1.5 million
ha of degraded land through afforestation and reforestation under
the Bonn Challenge by 2030 (Ministry of Agriculture, 2021; Ministry of
Ecology and Natural Resources, 2023).

As part of its NDC, Kazakhstan will implement measures to protect,
restore, and sustainably manage wetlands, with quantitative targets to
be reflected in future NDC and NAP updates.
3.2. Climate change projections
Applying climate projections to adaptation planning requires developing
plausible scenarios of future change and disaggregating trends by
geography and season to capture the complex pathways through which
climate impacts can affect human well-being and the larger national
economy.
3.2.1. Projected changes in temperature and precipitation
Climate scenarios do not diverge greatly by mid-century, suggesting
warming of between one- and two-degrees C. After mid-century, the
two scenarios evaluated for this NDC (RCP 4.5 and RCP 7.0) diverged

Kazakhstan recognizes that protecting and restoring
freshwater wetlands – rivers, lakes, and peatlands
– delivers co-benefits for both mitigation and

Kazakhstan became a member of the Freshwater

The analysis focused on two plausible future scenarios: RCP 4.5
and RCP 7.0. The analysis selected two scenarios to provide the
opportunity to assess impacts and the likely efficacy of adaptation
measures across a range of plausible futures.
Various reports conclude that surface air temperatures
in Kazakhstan will rise through 2100.

significantly, with the RCP 7.0 scenario reaching over 1.5 °C warmer
than the RCP 4.5 scenario by the end of the century. Warming will be
most pronounced in the summer, a principal agricultural season in
Kazakhstan, and the greatest warming will be experienced in the north
and northeastern regions of the country where most grain is cultivated.
While Kazakhstan is projected to see increases in annual precipitation, in
the summer, parts of the country will see seasonal declines in precipitation.
Under RCP 4.5, these decreases are concentrated in the northern and
eastern parts of the country, particularly in some regions responsible for
wheat production. Under RCP 7.0, decreases spread more broadly across
the northeast and eastern parts of the country in the second half of the
21st Century.
Mountain regions in the eastern part of the country may initially face
increased flood risk from enhanced river flows due to snowmelt, but this
risk could diminish later in the century as snowpack shrinks and shifts to
rain-dominated runoff. Heatwaves, however, are likely to become more
frequent and prolonged under both emissions scenarios.

4.1. Overview of loss and damage
As a vast, land-locked developing country exposed to increasing climate
extremes, Kazakhstan is already experiencing severe impacts, including
devastating floods, wildfires, droughts, and record-breaking heat that
damage infrastructure, disrupt food and energy systems, and threaten
lives and livelihoods.
The Government recognizes that these climate-related challenges
demand not only stronger mitigation and adaptation efforts but also
dedicated measures to avert, minimize, and address loss and damage
(L&D).
Kazakhstan is committed to protecting the most vulnerable populations,
including low-income households, women, children, elderly persons,
persons with disabilities, and farmers, whose livelihoods are most at risk.
Kazakhstan recognizes the mobility consequences of climate impacts,
including temporary and permanent internal displacement, and planned
relocation.
L&D in Kazakhstan stems from both sudden-onset hazards – floods,
droughts, wildfires, dust storms, heatwaves, and mudslides, and slow-onset
processes such as rising temperatures, shifting precipitation patterns,
land degradation, soil salinization, water scarcity, and biodiversity loss.
These impacts cause both economic losses, including infrastructure
damage, agricultural decline, and business disruption, and non-economic
losses, such as loss of lives, ecosystems, cultural heritage, and traditional
knowledge, many of which are irreplaceable.
Going forward, Kazakhstan intends to strengthen existing efforts to
minimize the impacts of floods, droughts, fires and other emergencies,
while integrating loss and damage issues into national planning.
55
The country’s participation as an alternate member of the Fund
for Responding Loss&Damage reflects its intention to strengthen
access to international technical assistance and finance while
bringing Central Asia’s unique challenges to global attention.

4.2. Determining needs
4.2.1. Economic losses and damages
Kazakhstan’s rising losses and damages from recent extreme weather
events underscore the urgency of mobilizing both domestic and
international resources to strengthen preparedness and recovery, protect
vulnerable populations, and avert further irreversible damage.
Economic losses from disasters have grown dramatically in recent years,
reflecting both intensifying hazards and gaps in resilience. Between 2020
and 2024, Kazakhstan incurred approximately USD 2 billion in damages,
averaging 0.24% of GDP annually, nearly 50 times higher than losses
recorded in 2015–2019.
Future risks are projected to rise, particularly for floods and heatwaves.
Under an intermediate emissions scenario, SSP2-4.5 ¹, high-hazard flood
risks may triple and long-duration heatwaves could increase six-fold by
2100, with even higher risks under high-emission pathways.
Based on historic loss patterns and climate projections, cumulative
damages for sudden onset events between 2026-2035 are estimated at
USD 1.5–5 billion, primarily affecting agriculture, water resources, energy
systems, and infrastructure.
These trends demonstrate the urgent need for scaled-up investment in
resilient infrastructure, early-warning systems, climate-smart agriculture,
and social protection measures to safeguard development gains.

4.2.2. Non-economic losses and damages
Non-economic harms are wide-ranging, from deterioration of health and
displacement to loss of cultural identity and ecosystem services.
The desiccation of the Aral Sea, while largely human-induced, has led to
collapsed livelihoods, biodiversity decline, and extensive health impacts,
and is now compounded by climate change through intensified dust
storms and salinization.
These are but a few examples of the ongoing climate-related impacts
facing the country.
Vulnerable groups, including women, children, older persons, persons
with disabilities, and low-income households, face disproportionate
impacts due to limited adaptive capacity and heightened exposure.
While these harms are not easily quantifiable, they are reflective of
enduring dimensions of Kazakhstan’s L&D.
4.3. Enabling legal framework for addressing
loss and damage
Kazakhstan’s existing legislation provides a strong foundation for
integrating climate-related loss and damage considerations into national
planning and response.
A number of sectoral laws and codes already address issues relevant to
climate risk management.
57
In the Turkistan region, water scarcity has eroded traditional
farming livelihoods and driven state-led relocation.
In western Kazakhstan, repeated floods have caused
permanent migration, while extreme heat and water
shortages in Mangystau have triggered psychological
distress and health impact.

Complementary provisions in the Water Code, Land Code, Forest Code,
and the Law on Cultural Heritage further reinforce resilience by providing
frameworks for the sustainable management of natural resources and
the protection of cultural assets.
These legal foundations, together with Kazakhstan’s international
commitments under the Paris Agreement and related frameworks, create
the basis for strengthening climate-specific L&D provisions, including
recognition of non-economic dimensions such as impacts on ecosystems,
cultural heritage, and public health. Future work will continue to build on
these instruments to ensure an integrated approach to addressing both
sudden- and slow-onset climate-related losses.
4.3.1. Social protection
Kazakhstan has put in place a range of social protection mechanisms
that help households and communities recover from climate-related
disasters.
These include:
- emergency food and cash assistance,
- temporary housing support for displaced populations,
- agricultural insurance schemes and
- loan deferral programs to support farmers affected by extreme
weather events.

Ongoing efforts aim to further align social protection systems with

4.3.2. Addressing loss and damage for climate-displaced
communities
Climate-related displacement is already a recognized phenomenon in
Kazakhstan. Resettlement initiatives have supported communities in
moving from regions facing acute water scarcity and environmental
pressures in the south to more secure areas in the north and east.
Integrating climate mobility considerations into adaptation and disaster
risk-reduction strategies is an important focus area.
This approach supports long-term resilience and enhances the
participation of relocated populations in decision-making, helping ensure
that future responses to displacement are well-planned, inclusive, and
sustainable.
4.4. Technical assistance and capacity
building needs to address L&D
Kazakhstan recognizes that, while important progress has been made
in integrating L&D into national disaster risk management and social
protection frameworks, further strengthening of institutional coordination,
data systems, and financing mechanisms is critical to respond effectively
to rising climate-related losses.
59
According to international assessments, climate-related internal
migration in Kazakhstan could affect between 3.1–4.6% of the
projected population (IOM 2023). Building on current experience,
Kazakhstan will develop subsidiary legislation and guidance
for planned relocation as a last resort, to ensure that relocation
processes are planned in a participatory way that safeguards the
rights, livelihoods, and cultural heritage of affected communities.

5.1. Institutional arrangement
The primary institutions responsible for NDC implementation and
achievement include:
The Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources of the Republic
of Kazakhstan (MENR) is the primary body for coordination and
implementation of the provisions of the Convention and the Paris
Agreement. It is a lead agency for climate change, environmental
protection, coordination of the UNFCCC and Paris Agreement
implementation.
MENR is the working body of the Council on the Transition to the Green
Economy, which is a coordinating body for sustainable development issues
like climate change. The Council focuses on monitoring and assessing the
implementation of the Concept for the Transition to a Green Economy,
and provides recommendations based on these assessments.
Furthermore, MENR is the leading institution in the Environmental Code
and a key partner in ETS regulation. MENR is also helping to develop
the National Adaptation Plan, setting forth adaptation strategies and
resiliency planning.
The Department of Climate Policy, within MENR, formulates and
coordinates state policy on climate and ozone layer protection. This
department also implements provisions of the UNFCCC and other
international agreements and oversees state policy on international
cooperation.
The Forestry and Wildlife Committee implements and supervises
functions related to forestry, wildlife protection, and use of specially
protected natural areas.
JSC Zhasyl Damu, a subsidiary of MENR, prepares the National
Greenhouse Gas Inventory Report annually for submission under the
UNFCCC.
Data collection is based on information from the Bureau of National
Statistics and official submissions from sectoral ministries. The
organization also serves as the operator of the national Emissions Trading
System, ensuring its administration, monitoring, and the development of
carbon regulation instruments. In addition, Zhasyl Damu contributes to
improving national climate policy and legislation and conducts analytical
studies to support evidence-based decision-making on greenhouse gas
emission regulation.
62

The Agency for Strategic Planning and Reforms, which houses the
Bureau of National Statistics and directly reports to the President,
analyses and disseminates statistical data for the national GHG inventory,
as well as data on other indicators to track progress towards the NDC
targets.
The Ministry of Energy is the body overseeing and implementing state
energy policy and planning in the Republic of Kazakhstan. Among other
things, it regulates production of petroleum products, gas and electricity
supply, nuclear energy and is central in developing renewable energy
sources.
Specific targets for renewable energy sources are also set forth in the
Strategic Plan of the Ministry of Energy of Kazakhstan for 2023-
2027, which establishes the goal of generating 50% of all energy by 2050
through expanding renewable energy capacity and storage, developing
nuclear energy projects, and investing in alternative energy sources.
The Action Plan for the Development of the Electric Power Industry
until 2035 is focused on increasing the share of renewable energy sources
in electricity generation, including wind power with energy storage, solar
power plants, and hydroelectricity.
The ETS Regulatory Body, which as previously mentioned is operated by
MENR, provides the legal and technical frameworks for the ETS, working
with partners like the PMI Trust Fund through a World Bank Initiative to
strengthen the ETS.
Another critical point of cross-sectoral coordination is planning documents
like the National Development Plan, which serve to integrate strategy
across economy, energy transition, and development goals, as well as the
strategic actions plans and their respective sectoral road maps, which link
investments and regulations to targets and strategies.
63
The Republic of Kazakhstan has a variety of interagency working
groups, such as those under MENR, that coordinate across ministries
to align on high-level climate and environmental policies. Youth
participation is being institutionalized through forums, working
groups, and representation in public councils. At least 30% youth
representation is ensured in decision-making bodies under the
Ministry of Ecology and at the local level.

5.2. Monitoring, reporting and verification
To accelerate NDC implementation, Kazakhstan aims to improve data
transparency, information, and analysis related to monitoring and
evaluation of climate data, as well as financial, technological, and capacity
building support.
The core of the national MRV system is the National Greenhouse Gas
Inventory, maintained by the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources.
Remote sensing (RS) and geographic information system (GIS) data play
a key role within the NIR system. The use of RS and GIS as tools for NIR
ensures the generation of reliable and objective data.
Their comprehensive integration into monitoring and reporting processes
enables the generation of long-term and comparable environmental data,
and their consistent application creates the basis for transparent and
verifiable national reporting, particularly for the National Greenhouse Gas
Inventory.
In this regard, unified sets of quality standards (quality assurance/quality
control) and data validation protocols will be developed to ensure the
consistency, reliability, and comparability of information used in national
monitoring, planning, and reporting systems.
These standards will form the basis for integrating climate data across
various agencies and ensure unified approaches to the development of
climate change reporting.
Progress on climate targets is also tracked through national statistical
and governance platforms. The Bureau of National Statistics and the
e-Government platform supply open data to government and the public
for oversight of government agencies’ progress on strategic development
plans. The Council on the Transition to a Green Economy, together with
the Ministry of Energy and the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources,
reviews the impacts of mitigation and adaptation measures.
64
A National Inventory Report has been prepared annually, tracking
emissions and removals since 1990.
The system is complemented by State Carbon and Waste
Inventories, a State Register of Carbon Units, and a Pollutant
Release and Transfer Register, which provide data for assessing the
effectiveness of national climate policy.

5.3. Support needs to enhance NDC
implementation capacities
Advanced technologies can catalyze renewable energy deployment,
carbon capture and storage, smart grids, water-saving technologies, and
deep electrification and weatherization.
Investing in capacity building, through actions like promoting
international best practices and providing training and educational
seminars to disseminate information around “green” transition and low-
carbon technologies, can help develop critical local expertise, improve
policy implementation, and implement projects in key sectors such as
energy, industry, and agriculture.
Kazakhstan has demonstrated strong domestic commitment,
financing the bulk of its mitigation and adaptation measures from
its own budget and state-owned enterprises.
Yet, achieving the ambition of NDC 3.0 and the 2060 Carbon-Neutrality
Strategy will require significantly more external support.
Key priorities for international assistance include:
• Financing the transition - concessional lending, equity, grants and
blended-finance facilities to modernize ageing infrastructure, scale
up renewables and energy efficiency, expand climate-resilient water,
transport and urban systems, and crowd-in private investment.
• Technology transfer and capacity-building - access to advanced
low-carbon technologies (hydrogen, CCUS, grid integration, drought-
resilient farming, efficient heating/cooling) and training of national
experts to deploy and maintain them.
65
Technology transfer is imperative to advancing mitigation,
adaptation, and a larger shift toward a low-carbon economy.
At the same time, capacity building is essential for implementing
mitigation and adaptation measures as mentioned in the NDC and
establishing the requisite technical expertise for technology transfer
to be effective.

• Just transition support - planning and implementing measures to
reskill workers, diversify coal-dependent regional economies, and
provide targeted social-protection schemes.
• MRV and data systems - building a unified national system for GHG
inventories (built on high-tier methods and approaches), mitigation
and adaptation tracking, including modernized reporting tools and
interoperable data platforms.
5.4. Strengthening Kazakhstan’s emissions
trading system as a core market-based
instrument
Kazakhstan operates the region’s only Emissions Trading System,
which currently covers the power and industrial sectors. Broadening ETS
coverage and increasing carbon pricing can generate new revenue while
driving emissions reductions.
The Environmental Code (2021, amended 2025) provides a modern legal
basis for the ETS. It defines the role of the Ministry of Ecology and Natural
Resources as the competent authority, for delivering cost-effective
mitigation.
With continued reform, stronger integration with Article 6 mechanisms,
and enhanced market confidence, it can mobilise domestic and
international finance for low-carbon transition while ensuring that
Kazakhstan’s NDC targets are met in an efficient and transparent manner.
These developments will ensure consistent carbon-price signals,
administrative efficiency, and compatibility between market-based and
fiscal instruments.

5.5. Article 6 cooperative approaches
Kazakhstan recognizes the role of cooperative approaches under Article
6 as a key instrument to help achieve its NDC targets while catalyzing
investment and innovation for sustainable development.
Amendments to the Environmental Code (2025) provide a dedicated
legal basis for implementing both Article 6.2 (bilateral/club-based
cooperation) and Article 6.4 (UNFCCC-supervised mechanism), as well as
for establishing a voluntary carbon market (VCM).
Key elements include:
• Legal definitions of ITMOs, corresponding adjustments (CA), “baseline
scenario,” “additionality,” and provisions for voluntary markets.
• Clear mandates for the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources
(MENR) as the national authority and for Jasyl Damu JSC as the
operator of the carbon market and national registry.
• Rules for accounting, registration, issuance, and transfer of units,
including a buffer account to hedge against natural risks (fires, drought)
and safeguard environmental integrity.
• Alignment with CMA decisions 2/CMA.3 and 3/CMA.3 (Glasgow
2021) to ensure transparency, prevent double counting, and uphold
sustainable-development safeguards.
An Article 6 Technical Working Group under MENR, comprising relevant
ministries (energy, finance, economy, industry, agriculture, foreign affairs),
sub-national authorities, and private-sector stakeholders, which reviews
project methodologies, approves baseline parameters, and advises on
authorizations. This governance architecture enables Kazakhstan to
participate credibly in international carbon markets and to integrate
Article 6 into national mitigation planning.
The country has already:
• Signed bilateral cooperation agreements with Japan and the Republic
of Korea, focused on developing rules, guidelines and institutional
arrangements for ITMO transfers.
• Committed to its NDC to explore ETS-linkage and other cooperative
mechanisms that can help mobilize carbon finance and accelerate
transition in key sectors.
71

The Republic of Kazakhstan recognizes that participation in the Article 6
mechanisms of the Paris Agreement should be strategic and phased in
order to avoid “overselling” the emission reductions needed to achieve
its own NDC targets, while maximizing the socio-economic benefits of
incoming carbon finance.
5.5.1. Key participation requirements for
Article 6 projects
To maintain environmental integrity and avoid double counting, all
cooperative-approach activities must, inter alia:
• Demonstrate additionality beyond policies and actions already
included in Kazakhstan’s NDC or ETS baseline.
• Apply approved international methodologies and national baseline
parameters validated by the Article 6 Technical Working Group.
• Ensure robust MRV systems integrated with the national GHG inventory
and registry.
• Contribute to sustainable-development co-benefits (e.g., job creation,
technology transfer, gender and youth inclusion).
• Implement social and environmental safeguards and respect
community and indigenous rights where applicable.
• Comply with national rules for corresponding adjustments to maintain
accuracy of Kazakhstan’s carbon budget.
Activities that are included in the unconditional target of Kazakhstan’s
NDC or that are already included in the ETS without clearly demonstrated
additionality are not eligible for participation in Article 6 mechanisms.

In Table 7, the LULUCF sector estimates include restoration of natural and
saxaul forests, while the waste sector estimates reflect the total annual
cost of waste management, taking into account technological improve-
ments and efficiency gains.
6.2. Domestic public finance
6.2.1. Role of national and local government budgets
Kazakhstan has made substantial domestic investments in climate action,
often without significant international financial support.
Despite being a land-locked developing country facing acute climate
vulnerabilities, frequent floods, droughts, wildfires, and severe heatwaves.
Kazakhstan has largely financed its mitigation and adaptation measures
from national and local budgets, supplemented by quasi-state and private
enterprise contributions.
Kazakhstan’s fiscal system is highly centralised: the republican budget
accounts for over 70 % of consolidated public expenditure and remains the
primary channel for direct public spending on climate-related priorities.

At the same time, local budgets play a frontline role in delivering
adaptation services, including flood management, waste collection, and
disaster-risk reduction, but remain heavily dependent on transfers from
the republican budget.
These expenditures demonstrate Kazakhstan’s considerable domestic
contribution toward addressing climate change.
The strategy for achieving carbon neutrality by 2060 also assumes that
the bulk of future investments will continue to come from businesses
(including state-owned companies) and households, while concessional
and grant external financing will remain limited.
In recent years, these targeted transfers have increasingly been directed
toward climate-sensitive infrastructure, including:
• sustainable water supply systems,
• climate and natural hazard mitigation facilities,
• modernization of key energy facilities.
Despite such significant domestic spending, Kazakhstan’s access to
international climate finance remains limited compared to the scale of
national needs, highlighting the importance of strengthening global
solidarity to complement national efforts.
76
Kazakhstan’s domestic spending on environmental protection,
already significant, far outweighs the external climate finance it has
received.

Kazakhstan’s SOEs have played a critical role in mobilising domestic capital
for low-carbon transition, supplementing limited international finance.
These instruments highlight the country’s significant self-funded
