Priority actions: Improve use of GIS and digital tools for risk mapping and integrate AI-based analytics for early warning and monitoring.
Improve access to reliable climate information, develop user-oriented climate services, and promote data-sharing between research institutions, ministries, and the public.
The forthcoming National Adaptation Plan and the National Development Plan to 2029 will further integrate climate objectives into sectoral and territorial development planning.

Climate scenarios do not diverge greatly by mid-century, suggesting warming of between one- and two-degrees C. After mid-century, the two scenarios evaluated for this NDC (RCP 4.5 and RCP 7.0) diverged

The analysis focused on two plausible future scenarios: RCP 4.5 and RCP 7.0. The analysis selected two scenarios to provide the opportunity to assess impacts and the likely efficacy of adaptation measures across a range of plausible futures.
Various reports conclude that surface air temperatures in Kazakhstan will rise through 2100.

significantly, with the RCP 7.0 scenario reaching over 1.5 °C warmer than the RCP 4.5 scenario by the end of the century. Warming will be most pronounced in the summer, a principal agricultural season in Kazakhstan, and the greatest warming will be experienced in the north and northeastern regions of the country where most grain is cultivated.
While Kazakhstan is projected to see increases in annual precipitation, in the summer, parts of the country will see seasonal declines in precipitation. Under RCP 4.5, these decreases are concentrated in the northern and eastern parts of the country, particularly in some regions responsible for wheat production. Under RCP 7.0, decreases spread more broadly across the northeast and eastern parts of the country in the second half of the 21st Century.
Mountain regions in the eastern part of the country may initially face increased flood risk from enhanced river flows due to snowmelt, but this risk could diminish later in the century as snowpack shrinks and shifts to rain-dominated runoff. Heatwaves, however, are likely to become more frequent and prolonged under both emissions scenarios.

As a vast, land-locked developing country exposed to increasing climate extremes, Kazakhstan is already experiencing severe impacts, including devastating floods, wildfires, droughts, and record-breaking heat that damage infrastructure, disrupt food and energy systems, and threaten lives and livelihoods.
The Government recognizes that these climate-related challenges demand not only stronger mitigation and adaptation efforts but also dedicated measures to avert, minimize, and address loss and damage (L&D).

L&D in Kazakhstan stems from both sudden-onset hazards – floods, droughts, wildfires, dust storms, heatwaves, and mudslides, and slow-onset processes such as rising temperatures, shifting precipitation patterns, land degradation, soil salinization, water scarcity, and biodiversity loss. These impacts cause both economic losses, including infrastructure damage, agricultural decline, and business disruption, and non-economic losses, such as loss of lives, ecosystems, cultural heritage, and traditional knowledge, many of which are irreplaceable.
Going forward, Kazakhstan intends to strengthen existing efforts to minimize the impacts of floods, droughts, fires and other emergencies, while integrating loss and damage issues into national planning.

Economic losses from disasters have grown dramatically in recent years, reflecting both intensifying hazards and gaps in resilience. Between 2020 and 2024, Kazakhstan incurred approximately USD 2 billion in damages, averaging 0.24% of GDP annually, nearly 50 times higher than losses recorded in 2015–2019.

Based on historic loss patterns and climate projections, cumulative damages for sudden onset events between 2026-2035 are estimated at USD 1.5–5 billion, primarily affecting agriculture, water resources, energy systems, and infrastructure.
The table below outlines key priority areas for action to reduce vulnerability and enable swift and inclusive recovery from future loss and damage events.
Loss assessment Develop processes for Post-Disaster Needs Assessments (PDNAs) to quantify financial losses and prioritize recovery
Financial instruments Shock-responsive social protection, contingency funds, disaster risk insurance, catastrophe bonds
Institutional coordination Strengthened coordination across Ministry of Emergency Situations, Ministry of Ecology, and subnational agencies; regional and international coordination
Fiscal integration Pre-allocated contingency reserves, disaster reserve funds, recovery frameworks in national budgets
Development planning Integrate non-economic L&D into adaptation planning and disaster risk preparedness
Capacity building Develop institutional capacities for L&D assessment, especially at local authority level; utilize Santiago Network support
Legal framework Protect vulnerable group rights; enact legislation for planned relocation and land tenure security
Livelihood diversification Support reskilling and alternative non-climate-sensitive livelihood options
Biodiversity protection Monitor ecosystem service losses; implement ecosystem-based adaptation and nature-based solutions
Cultural preservation Recognize Indigenous knowledge; preserve cultural heritage in legislation and practice

Kazakhstan is committed to protecting the most vulnerable populations, including low-income households, women, children, elderly persons, persons with disabilities, and farmers, whose livelihoods are most at risk.
Kazakhstan recognizes the mobility consequences of climate impacts, including temporary and permanent internal displacement, and planned relocation.

In 2023 alone, Kazakhstan’s environmental and climate-related spending exceeded USD 1.3 billion, complemented by significant capital investments in renewable energy, resilient water infrastructure, disaster risk management and other priority sectors.
To meet the investment needs of NDC 3.0 and achieve a resilient, low-carbon transition, Kazakhstan emphasizes the need for larger volumes and more diverse international financing:
predictable and longer-term external finance to complement domestic investment;
stronger grant-based support and concessional lending for adaptation, nature-based solutions, and just transition measures;
equity investments, risk-sharing schemes, subordinated and mezzanine loans;
technology transfer and partnerships for advanced mitigation options such as hydrogen, CCUS, grid integration and climate-smart agriculture.

Kazakhstan calls on the international community and its partners to better align climate finance flows with national needs and to ensure that countries with high climate ambition but limited access to concessional funding receive the support necessary to deliver on their NDC commitments.

The Environmental Code (2021) provides the legal basis for climate action, introducing emission-reduction principles, climate-related permitting, and green-finance mechanisms. It underpins the National Emissions Trading System (ETS) and mandates a gradual decline in the national carbon budget, with revenues from allowance payments channeled toward environmental projects. These complementary strategies, plans and instruments together constitute the backbone of Kazakhstan’s climate-policy architecture. The long-term Strategy on Achieving Carbon Neutrality by 2060 defines the destination, the medium-term plans translate it into investment priorities, the Environmental Code provides the legal foundation, and the ETS introduces a market signal for reducing emissions.

Kazakhstan commits to reduce economy-wide net greenhouse gas emissions, including LULUCF, by 17 percent below 1990 levels by 2035 as an unconditional target, and up to 25 percent below 1990 by 2035 conditional on timely international finance, technology transfer, and capacity-building. The targets adopt the 2026–2035 common time frame, cover all IPCC sectors and gases (CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, HFCs, PFCs, SF₆, NF₃), and apply IPCC 2006 Guidelines with AR5 GWPs.

• 320 Mt CO₂-equivalent by 2035 (about 17 percent below 1990 levels,

The conditional pathway builds on the unconditional mitigation commitment with deeper decarbonisation enabled by international partnerships and investment. It foresees net emissions reaching about 288 Mt CO₂-equivalent by 2035, roughly about 32 percent below BAU and broadly consistent with the conditional ambition level in NDC 2.0, which is 25%.

NDC target of Kazakhstan covers all sectors and gases consistent with the IPCC guidelines that are covered by the national GHG inventory as follows:
- Sectors as defined by the IPCC guidelines in accordance with decision 18/CMA.1, namely Energy, Industrial processes and product use (IPPU), Agriculture, Land Use, Land Use Change and Forestry (LULUCF) and Waste;

- The LULUCF categories and pools are those included in the IPCC 2006 guidelines and occurring in Kazakhstan.

The LULUCF sector, once a net sink, became a net source with 3.3 Mt CO₂e in 2023, though emissions declined 28.9% from 2021, indicating improved land management.

findings.text: The document projects average temperature increases of 1.7–1.9°C before 2030, 2.4–3.1°C by 2050, and 3.2–6.0°C before 2100; the range endpoints correspond to RCP4.5 and RCP8.5. It also describes increasing dry-period frequency, reduced mountain snowfall and further glacier melt.

citations.quote: Further temperature increases are expected on average by 1.7-1.9°C before 2030 and 2.4-3.1°C by 2050, increasing by 3.2-6.0°C before 2100. The lower limit of the range corresponds to the scenario of greenhouse gas concentrations RCP4.5, and the upper limit to RCP8.5. Along with an increase in precipitation during the winter months, the country is likely to experience an increase in the frequency and intensity of dry periods in other seasons. In mountainous areas, even with an increase in precipitation, higher temperatures will lead to a reduction in precipitation in the form of snow and further melting of glaciers.

findings.text: The document reports droughts of varying severity affecting more than half of Kazakhstan’s land area in two out of every five years since 2000, and identifies growing water scarcity and desertification as among the most serious climate-change consequences.

citations.quote:
Since 2000, droughts of varying severity have already affected more than 50% of the total land area of Kazakhstan in two out of every five years. The likely consequences include the continued expansion of deserts and arid areas with the possible loss of coastline due to the lowering of the Caspian Sea level. On the other hand, the increase in severe storms with intense rains will cause an increase in the frequency of river floods, overrunning events and the number of flash floods and mudslides.
The most serious consequences of climate change include growing water scarcity and desertification.

findings.text: The document identifies gaps in adaptation planning, monitoring and reporting: inadequate institutional and technical support for mainstreaming, no permanent cross-ministry and cross-region discussion platform, incomplete climate-information inventories, fragmented and outdated vulnerability assessments, a need to harmonize data methods, and insufficient trained personnel. It says these gaps will be addressed through the Environmental Code and adopted plans and programmes.

citations.quote: Existing gaps and barriers to climate change adaptation (CCA) planning, monitoring, and reporting in Kazakhstan comprise insufficient institutional and technical support for mainstreaming adaptation into sectoral and local development plans, lack of permanent inter-ministerial and cross-regional platform for discussion of adaptation issues, lack of inventories of existing climate information, combined with fragmented and outdated vulnerability assessments, strong need to harmonize techniques for climate-related data collection, analysis and documentation, lack of required trained personnel (numbers and expertise) to meet adaptation objectives. These gaps and barriers will be addressed in the course of implementing the provisions of the Environmental Code and in the process of implementing the adopted programs and plans.

findings.text: The government has established annual monitoring and reporting on the 2021–2030 Green Economy Action Plan. A similar monitoring mechanism for the NDC Roadmap is to be established once it is adopted; Roadmap implementation is planned for review every five years, using sector indicators and, where possible, scientific data.

citations.quote: A system of annual monitoring and reporting on the implementation of the 2021-2030 Action Plan has been established by the Government of the Republic of Kazakhstan Resolution No 479 of 29 July 2020 on the Action Plan for the implementation of the Concept for the transition of the Republic of Kazakhstan to a “Green Economy” for 2021-2030.

A similar mechanism will be established to monitor the implementation of the Roadmap for the NDC implementation when it is adopted.
Evaluation of the implementation of the Roadmap for NDC implementation will culminate in a review every five years, enabling corrective planning and implementation of further measures. findings.text: The document describes the unified climate platform, digital monitoring, satellite data and intelligent systems as planned means to improve emissions and land-use information, support MRV, and report NDC progress in Biennial Transparency Reports. It also says local experts developed modelling capabilities during NDC and long-term strategy preparation, supporting future assessment and policy advice.

citations.quote:
Achievement of NDC targets and carbon neutrality will demand holistic digitalization first of all in the energy sector and the environment to track a carbon footprint and to ensure transparency as well as the creation of an innovation ecosystem both for applied research programs and new financial tools on decarbonization.
Introducing intelligent systems in the power sector will touch all levels of the energy sector – systematic management, power generation, and distribution and it will enable the creation of conditions to integrate renewables (RES) and distributed generation and also strengthen the sustainability of the system due to better monitoring and maintenance. The use of satellite data and intelligent systems will enable to track and monitor any changes in land use and forests and will improve the quality of data collection. Digitalization of the energy system, large emitters and land users and other sectors in the manner of a united climate platform will provide operational access to credible and complete information on the data of both greenhouse gas emissions and other pollutants that will ensure credibility and coherence of the climate system of the Republic of Kazakhstan and will be a crucial element for the Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (MRV) system, and will increase trust from potential partners and citizens. Monitoring of the NDC implementation progress will be reported in the Biennial transparency report including the progress of the current plans and programs implementation, policy and practical indicators by using available data of the unified climate platform.

To prepare the NDC of the Republic of Kazakhstan, a team of national and international experts used advanced decision support tools, including a macroeconomic general equilibrium model and a technical and economic model of the entire energy system. During the preparation of the NDC and the long-term low-emission development strategy, local experts built up their competencies in the development and use of integrated models for long-term energy planning, macroeconomic modelling and systems analysis. findings.text: The NDC Roadmap concept or programme document was planned for development in 2022–2024 and was to define relevant research priorities, education and skills programmes, research partnerships and centres, and an ecosystem for new decarbonization solutions. The document also states that technical assistance to build local multidisciplinary expertise, train scientists and organize professional exchanges would support climate policy and decarbonization.

figures.label: Planned NDC Roadmap document development period

citations.quote:
To ensure the achievement of NDC, it will be necessary to conduct a variety of assessment and foresight studies on the needs of the long-term low-carbon development of the Republic of Kazakhstan with the involvement of stakeholders using various methods to generate trans-disciplinary ideas. In 2022-2024, a concept or a program document for the NDC Roadmap will be developed, defining:
1. Key thematic areas, and research relevant to the Republic of Kazakhstan based on the R&D portfolio management approach, identifying promising topics and screening out low-impact projects.
2. competencies, courses and programs of formal education for the needs of decarbonization, and options for implementing digital multidisciplinary postgraduate education programs, including in partnership with foreign universities and online education platforms.
3. ways for integration and cooperation of organizations and industry with universities, by funding research programmes fellowships, setting up research centres focussing on sustainable development and carbon neutrality to prepare highly experienced personnel and carry out studies and research on decarbonization, taking into account the national circumstances.
4. approaches for creating an ecosystem for the development of new decarbonization solutions, including startup incubators and (or)
integration with the existing ones.

It is worth noting that additional technical assistance to build local expert multidisciplinary potential, train scientific personnel, organize professional exchange programs will play a critical role in strengthening climate policy and implementing decarbonization.

citations.quote: Afforestation and reforestation mitigation outcomes under three different scenarios until 2030 were modelled with the use of CBM-CFS3 (Carbon Budget Model of the Canadian Forest Sector) software. In the first three years [after planting] each hectare of coniferous, soft-wooded, or hardwood trees absorbs the average of 1 ton of carbon per year that is equivalent to 3.67 tons of CO2 per year per hectare subject to lack of disturbances. However, later this parameter drops to 0.7 tons of carbon per year per forest hectare. This can be explained by forest aging which is leading to a decrease in carbon dioxide absorption. The 25-year lifespan of commercial forests will provide the country with adaptation benefits (water retention, wood for construction, etc.) as well as increase carbon sinks offsetting anthropogenic emissions that cannot be further mitigated or reduced by other means.

citations.quote: The Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources of the Republic of Kazakhstan (hereinafter – the Ministry) is responsible since 2019 for developing and coordinating climate change policy. Climate policy planning and implementation is supported by the Ministry in cooperation with relevant sectoral ministries. Mainstreaming climate change and climate adaptation will depend on close cooperation between the ministries.

The Development Strategy of the Republic of Kazakhstan until 2050 (hereinafter – Strategy 2050) (Statement of the President of the Republic of Kazakhstan dated 14 December 2012) and the Concept for the transition of the Republic of Kazakhstan to a green economy (hereinafter – Concept) (Decree of the President of the Republic of Kazakhstan #577 dated 30 May 2013) are the starting points for the implementation of climate policy, laying the foundations for deep systemic transformation in order to transition to green economy, improving the welfare and quality of life of the population while minimizing the footprint on the environment and degradation of natural resources. In particular, long-term goals are being set, such as reducing the energy intensity of GDP from the 2008 level by 50% by 2050, and increasing the share of alternative sources in electricity generation to 50% by 2050.

Since 2000, droughts of varying severity have already affected more than 50% of the total land area of Kazakhstan in two out of every five years. The likely consequences include the continued expansion of deserts and arid areas with the possible loss of coastline due to the lowering of the Caspian Sea level. On the other hand, the increase in severe storms with intense rains will cause an increase in the frequency of river floods, overrunning events and the number of flash floods and mudslides.
The most serious consequences of climate change include growing water scarcity and desertification.

Existing gaps and barriers to climate change adaptation (CCA) planning, monitoring, and reporting in Kazakhstan comprise insufficient institutional and technical support for mainstreaming adaptation into sectoral and local development plans, lack of permanent inter-ministerial and cross-regional platform for discussion of adaptation issues, lack of inventories of existing climate information, combined with fragmented and outdated vulnerability assessments, strong need to harmonize techniques for climate-related data collection, analysis and documentation, lack of required trained personnel (numbers and expertise) to meet adaptation objectives. These gaps and barriers will be addressed in the course of implementing the provisions of the Environmental Code and in the process of implementing the adopted programs and plans.

A system of annual monitoring and reporting on the implementation of the 2021-2030 Action Plan has been established by the Government of the Republic of Kazakhstan Resolution No 479 of 29 July 2020 on the Action Plan for the implementation of the Concept for the transition of the Republic of Kazakhstan to a “Green Economy” for 2021-2030.

A similar mechanism will be established to monitor the implementation of the Roadmap for the NDC implementation when it is adopted.
Evaluation of the implementation of the Roadmap for NDC implementation will culminate in a review every five years, enabling corrective planning and implementation of further measures. The success of implementation will be judged against a set of indicators specific for each sector. Apart from reports submitted by public administration bodies on an annual basis, scientific data will be used, where possible.

Achievement of NDC targets and carbon neutrality will demand holistic digitalization first of all in the energy sector and the environment to track a carbon footprint and to ensure transparency as well as the creation of an innovation ecosystem both for applied research programs and new financial tools on decarbonization.
Introducing intelligent systems in the power sector will touch all levels of the energy sector – systematic management, power generation, and distribution and it will enable the creation of conditions to integrate renewables (RES) and distributed generation and also strengthen the sustainability of the system due to better monitoring and maintenance. The use of satellite data and intelligent systems will enable to track and monitor any changes in land use and forests and will improve the quality of data collection. Digitalization of the energy system, large emitters and land users and other sectors in the manner of a united climate platform will provide operational access to credible and complete information on the data of both greenhouse gas emissions and other pollutants that will ensure credibility and coherence of the climate system of the Republic of Kazakhstan and will be a crucial element for the Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (MRV) system, and will increase trust from potential partners and citizens. Monitoring of the NDC implementation progress will be reported in the Biennial transparency report including the progress of the current plans and programs implementation, policy and practical indicators by using available data of the unified climate platform.

To prepare the NDC of the Republic of Kazakhstan, a team of national and international experts used advanced decision support tools, including a macroeconomic general equilibrium model and a technical and economic model of the entire energy system. During the preparation of the NDC and the long-term low-emission development strategy, local experts built up their competencies in the development and use of integrated models for long-term energy planning, macroeconomic modelling and systems analysis. In the future, this will allow for regular assessment of current decarbonization rates, reassessment of development plans, proposals for government policy improvements, and expert decision-making support for the development and

To ensure the achievement of NDC, it will be necessary to conduct a variety of assessment and foresight studies on the needs of the long-term low-carbon development of the Republic of Kazakhstan with the involvement of stakeholders using various methods to generate trans-disciplinary ideas. In 2022-2024, a concept or a program document for the NDC Roadmap will be developed, defining:
1. Key thematic areas, and research relevant to the Republic of Kazakhstan based on the R&D portfolio management approach, identifying promising topics and screening out low-impact projects.
2. competencies, courses and programs of formal education for the needs of decarbonization, and options for implementing digital multidisciplinary postgraduate education programs, including in partnership with foreign universities and online education platforms.
3. ways for integration and cooperation of organizations and industry with universities, by funding research programmes fellowships, setting up research centres focussing on sustainable development and carbon neutrality to prepare highly experienced personnel and carry out studies and research on decarbonization, taking into account the national circumstances.
4. approaches for creating an ecosystem for the development of new decarbonization solutions, including startup incubators and (or)
integration with the existing ones.

It is worth noting that additional technical assistance to build local expert multidisciplinary potential, train scientific personnel, organize professional exchange programs will play a critical role in strengthening climate policy and implementing decarbonization.
2. Lack of access to cheap loans for low-carbon projects, while brown assets have access to guarantees and financing with a potentially lower interest rate.
3. Lack of consideration of climate criteria and criteria of Sustainable Development Goals in the budgetary process, which leads to risks of financing and potentially stranded assets.

At the same time, it is necessary to significantly modernize science and education, increase research and human resources, establish programs for the development and transfer of critical technologies for low-carbon development, develop a portfolio approach for research in the field of decarbonization; reduce investment risks and establish mechanisms for obtaining cheap loans for capital-intensive low-carbon

The Republic of Kazakhstan aims to achieve carbon neutrality by 2060, which contributes to the accelerated achievement of the global peak of greenhouse gas emissions in the first half of the 21st century and also takes into account the constraints imposed by the principles of equity, sustainable development and poverty eradication.

Kazakhstan pledged to restore at least up to 1.5 million ha of degraded land through afforestation and reforestation until 2030 under the Bonn Challenge. Afforestation of at least up to 1.5 million ha of degraded land under the Bonn Challenge would bring substantial mitigation benefits. Forestry planting programmes will, apart from boosting carbon sequestration on an unprecedented level, support land rehabilitation projects, convert unproductive land to forestry, rejuvenate damaged landscapes and create jobs in the sustainable forestry and timber industry.

Afforestation and reforestation mitigation outcomes under three different scenarios until 2030 were modelled with the use of CBM-CFS3 (Carbon Budget Model of the Canadian Forest Sector) software. In the first three years [after planting] each hectare of coniferous, soft-wooded, or hardwood trees absorbs the average of 1 ton of carbon per year that is equivalent to 3.67 tons of CO2 per year per hectare subject to lack of disturbances. However, later this parameter drops to 0.7 tons of carbon per year per forest hectare. This can be explained by forest aging which is leading to a decrease in carbon dioxide absorption. The 25-year lifespan of commercial forests will provide the country with adaptation benefits (water retention, wood for construction, etc.) as well as increase carbon sinks offsetting anthropogenic emissions that cannot be further mitigated or reduced by other means.

To increase forest cover, the government is planning to improve in the 2022-
2030 period the mechanism of support incentivizing the setting up of private
industrial plantations and forest nurseries, and implementation of pilot projects
in this field supported by public-private partnerships. Further measures are
planned to ensure the protection of forests. In 2020, National Action Plan for
the implementation of the Address of the Head of State to the people of
Kazakhstan dated September 1, 2020 "Kazakhstan in a new reality: time for
action”. It aims to ensure planting of more than 2 billion trees in the forest
fund and 15 million in settlements within five years, and it is aligned with the
Bonn Challenge goals.

According to Article 283, the paragraph 3 of the Code the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources (hereinafter – MENR) has been designated as a working body for the implementation of international treaties in the field of climate change. MENR carries out state regulation in the field of greenhouse gas emissions and removals in order to ensure the achievement of the NDC of the Republic of Kazakhstan. Moreover, under the Article 283, paragraph 4 of the Code the state agencies of the Republic of Kazakhstan, within their competence, are obliged to take actions aimed at ensuring the NDC implementation.

Unconditional target:
Reduction of GHG emissions by 15% by the end of 2030 relative to 1990 base year.
Economy-wide absolute reduction.

Conditional target:
Reduction of GHG emissions by 25% by the end of 2030 relative to 1990 base year, subject to significant additional international investments and significant grant assistance; access to an international technology transfer mechanism; co-financing and participation in international research projects, development of promising low-carbon technologies and initiatives to build local expertise.
Economy-wide absolute reduction.

Emission coverage in accordance with Article 281, paragraph 2 of the Code:
carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O),
hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), perfluorocarbons (PFCs) and sulfur hexafluoride
(SF6), other substances identified by the authorized body in the field of
environment protection (in accordance with article 281 paragraph 3 of the
Code).
Sector coverage in accordance with the Intergovernmental Group of Experts
on Climate Change (hereinafter – IPCC) Guidelines for National Greenhouse
Gas Inventories, 2006: energy, industrial processes and product use,
agriculture, forestry and other land use, waste.

The reference indicator will be based on the data of 1990 – 2030 greenhouse gas emissions inventory of the Republic of Kazakhstan submitted to the United Nations Convention on Climate Change Secretariat (hereinafter – UNFCCC) in 2032.
Reference indicators will be reassessed in case of new data availability, changes in methodological approaches, use of national coefficients and other clarifications.
Data on 2030 emissions and NDC target achievement will be based on 1990-2030 inventory data available in 2032.

Methodological approaches are based on the use of the following methods:
1. IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse Gas Inventories, 2006.
2. 2013 Supplement to the 2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse
Gas Inventories: Wetlands.
3. 2019 Refinement to the 2006 IPCC Guidelines for National Greenhouse
Gas Inventories.
4. Global warming potential values according to recent available the
UNFCCC Decisions adopted.

Emissions as a result of natural anomalies on managed lands and emissions from harvested wood products, as well as approaches used, assumptions and their compliance with IPCC guidelines will be available in the National Greenhouse Gas Inventory Report.

The Republic of Kazakhstan is already experiencing the effects of climate change.
Air temperatures in Kazakhstan have increased significantly over the past few decades. The average annual temperature increased by 0.32°C every 10 years. The highest temperature was observed in 2020 when the average anomaly in the country was 1.92°C. These figures demonstrate that the average annual air temperature in Kazakhstan is growing faster than the global average.

Further temperature increases are expected on average by 1.7-1.9°C before 2030 and 2.4-3.1°C by 2050, increasing by 3.2-6.0°C before 2100. The lower limit of the range corresponds to the scenario of greenhouse gas concentrations RCP4.5, and the upper limit to RCP8.5. Along with an increase in precipitation during the winter months, the country is likely to experience an increase in the frequency and intensity of dry periods in other seasons. In mountainous areas, even with an increase in precipitation, higher temperatures will lead to a reduction in precipitation in the form of snow and further melting of glaciers.

by_document.summary: Reports an established civil-protection framework, existing recovery assistance and ongoing work on flood protection, hydrological observation, forecasting, monitoring and response. It also sets preparedness targets and proposes further loss assessment, recovery planning and risk-finance measures.

Describes disaster-risk-reduction governance and regional cooperation, climate-risk scenarios and vulnerabilities, and gaps in climate-risk information. It does not specify operational warning, response, recovery, risk-finance or dedicated flood-protection measures in the retrieved pages.

changes_between_editions.text: NDC2 describes progress aligned with the Sendai Framework, a national and sub-national legislative and institutional approach, and a regional center established in 2016. These governance details are not repeated in NDC1; NDC1 instead reports the Law on Civil Protection and proposes further coordination and integration into adaptation policies.

NDC1 adds specific ongoing and proposed measures for flood protection, observation and warning, civil protection, recovery and risk finance. These details are not repeated in NDC2; the available findings do not establish that the measures were withdrawn.

Both editions discuss climate-related disaster risks, but NDC2 describes observed climate impacts and broad projections, while NDC1 includes later event-loss records and projections of future disaster damages and flood risks.

citations.quote:
Economic losses from disasters have grown dramatically in recent years, reflecting both intensifying hazards and gaps in resilience. Between 2020 and 2024, Kazakhstan incurred approximately USD 2 billion in damages, averaging 0.24% of GDP annually, nearly 50 times higher than losses recorded in 2015–2019.
Future risks are projected to rise, particularly for floods and heatwaves. Under an intermediate emissions scenario, SSP2-4.5 ¹, high-hazard flood risks may triple and long-duration heatwaves could increase six-fold by 2100, with even higher risks under high-emission pathways.
Based on historic loss patterns and climate projections, cumulative damages for sudden onset events between 2026-2035 are estimated at USD 1.5–5 billion

citations.quote: the Law on Civil Protection (2014), which establishes a comprehensive national framework for emergency preparedness and disaster response.

Kazakhstan recognizes that, while important progress has been made in integrating L&D into national disaster risk management and social protection frameworks, further strengthening of institutional coordination, data systems, and financing mechanisms is critical to respond effectively to rising climate-related losses.

Mountain regions in the eastern part of the country may initially face increased flood risk from enhanced river flows due to snowmelt, but this risk could diminish later in the century as snowpack shrinks and shifts to rain-dominated runoff.

Economic losses from disasters have grown dramatically in recent years, reflecting both intensifying hazards and gaps in resilience. Between 2020 and 2024, Kazakhstan incurred approximately USD 2 billion in damages, averaging 0.24% of GDP annually, nearly 50 times higher than losses recorded in 2015–2019.
Future risks are projected to rise, particularly for floods and heatwaves. Under an intermediate emissions scenario, SSP2-4.5 ¹, high-hazard flood risks may triple and long-duration heatwaves could increase six-fold by 2100, with even higher risks under high-emission pathways.
Based on historic loss patterns and climate projections, cumulative damages for sudden onset events between 2026-2035 are estimated at USD 1.5–5 billion

citations.quote: Since the adoption of the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015-2030) by Kazakhstan progress has been made in implementing activities aligned with the four priorities of the Sendai Framework. These figures demonstrate that the average annual air temperature in Kazakhstan is growing faster than the global average.

Other key stress factors associated with climate change include an increase in the number and intensity of extreme weather events (heavy rain, heavy snowfall, storm and hail), drought and glaciers melting.

Further temperature increases are expected on average by 1.7-1.9°C before 2030 and 2.4-3.1°C by 2050, increasing by 3.2-6.0°C before 2100. The lower limit of the range corresponds to the scenario of greenhouse gas concentrations RCP4.5, and the upper limit to RCP8.5.
Since 2000, droughts of varying severity have already affected more than 50% of the total land area of Kazakhstan in two out of every five years.
On the other hand, the increase in severe storms with intense rains will cause an increase in the frequency of river floods, overrunning events and the number of flash floods and mudslides.

citations.quote: Existing gaps and barriers to climate change adaptation (CCA) planning, monitoring, and reporting in Kazakhstan comprise insufficient institutional and technical support for mainstreaming adaptation into sectoral and local development plans, lack of permanent inter-ministerial and cross-regional platform for discussion of adaptation issues, lack of inventories of existing climate information, combined with fragmented and outdated vulnerability assessments, strong need to harmonize techniques for climate-related data collection, analysis and documentation, lack of required trained personnel (numbers and expertise) to meet adaptation objectives.
These gaps and barriers will be addressed in the course of implementing the provisions of the Environmental Code and in the process of implementing the adopted programs and plans.

citations.quote: However, it is the anticipated increased frequency of natural disasters and emergencies, on top of the slow onset events, that will require mobilization of the government reaction and strengthening of the DRR component in the adaptation planning and implementation.

Since the adoption of the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015-2030) by Kazakhstan progress has been made in implementing activities aligned with the four priorities of the Sendai Framework. The DRR-related legislative and institutional framework will enable integrated mainstreaming of adaptation to climate change and risk management at both, national and sub-national levels, with the involvement of stakeholders such as vulnerable communities and youth, taking into account gender considerations and enhanced cooperation regionally, enabled through the Center for Emergency Situations and Disaster Risk Reduction, set up in Almaty in 2016 and serving Kazakhstan and its neighbors, Kyrgyzstan, and Afghanistan.

Air temperatures in Kazakhstan have increased significantly over the past few decades. The average annual temperature increased by 0.32°C every 10 years. The highest temperature was observed in 2020 when the average anomaly in the country was 1.92°C. These figures demonstrate that the average annual air temperature in Kazakhstan is growing faster than the global average.

Other key stress factors associated with climate change include an increase in the number and intensity of extreme weather events (heavy rain, heavy snowfall, storm and hail), drought and glaciers melting.

Further temperature increases are expected on average by 1.7-1.9°C before 2030 and 2.4-3.1°C by 2050, increasing by 3.2-6.0°C before 2100. The lower limit of the range corresponds to the scenario of greenhouse gas concentrations RCP4.5, and the upper limit to RCP8.5.
Since 2000, droughts of varying severity have already affected more than 50% of the total land area of Kazakhstan in two out of every five years.
On the other hand, the increase in severe storms with intense rains will cause an increase in the frequency of river floods, overrunning events and the number of flash floods and mudslides.
All big cities of Kazakhstan are situated on the banks of major rivers and therefore prone to flooding.
Extreme weather events resulting in floods or mudslides may critically endanger infrastructure such as roads, bridges, and buildings.

hydrogen as well as other alternative sources of energy.

Action plan on implementation of the election program of the President of the Republic of Kazakhstan “Just Kazakhstan – for all and everyone, Now and forever” adopted by the Decree of the President of the Republic of Kazakhstan # 2 dated 26 November 2022 contains the following activities that contribute to achieving the NDC target by 2030: to attract by 2029 not less than 150 billion USD worth of direct foreign investment; 60% gasification of the country area; 1,5 times increase of the volume of production using RES;
creation of a required infrastructure for EVs in large cities of the country.

41.3 percent of the population of Kazakhstan lives in rural settlements with poorly developed infrastructure, remote from industrial centers, with a small capacity of the domestic market and with a predominance of energy-intensive export-oriented sectors of the economy, which provide the main revenues of the state budget, and significantly affect economic policy and the exchange rate of the national currency. The Republic of Kazakhstan will need to introduce new and significantly strengthen existing carbon pricing mechanisms in order to achieve its NDC, which has a double dependence on fossil fuels (coal and oil) in the country.

It will also be necessary to increase the share of renewable energy sources (solar and wind) in the balance of electricity production, and to use previously unused capacities to increase the maneuverability of the system. It will be necessary to change the existing dispatching modes of the power grid to more adaptive ones, digitalize the aging energy fleet and introduce the use of digital twins.

The introduction of carbon pricing can lead to an increase in prices for fuel and energy resources and dependent services, and to a significant increase in inflation, which in turn can significantly worsen the welfare of the population.

Lack of consideration of climate criteria and criteria of Sustainable Development Goals in the budgetary process, which leads to risks of financing and potentially stranded assets.

The risk of a shortage of natural gas for decarbonization of energy. Achieving NDC targets implies an increase in natural gas supplies, which requires field development and investment, as well as tariff revisions.

At the same time, it is necessary to prevent an increase in inflation and a significant increase in energy tariffs and basic needs of the population; it is also necessary to take into account that external factors, such as the consequences of a worldwide pandemic, global market volatility, and instability in neighboring states have negative social and economic consequences for the economy and population of the Republic of Kazakhstan and significantly reduce the window of intervention and reforms even for achieving the current NDC target.

findings.text: The document states that the 2030 NDC and 2060 carbon-neutrality strategy are being harmonized with the long-term low-emission development strategy. Further harmonization of ecology, climate and energy policies will be considered, including scenarios for renewable energy and fossil-fuel shares; an updated draft NDC implementation roadmap was to be presented in 2023–2024.

citations.quote: Given the development of a long-term low-emission development strategy, NDC for 2030 and carbon neutrality strategy for 2060 are being harmonized. In 2023-2024, an updated draft of the Roadmap for NDC implementation will be presented, taking into account the main issues of long-term low-carbon development and harmonization with sectoral policies.

the Action Plan for the implementation of the Concept for the Transition of the Republic of Kazakhstan to a "green economy" for 2021-2030 (Enactment of the Government of the Republic of Kazakhstan #479 dated 29 July 2020), which provides for the implementation of necessary measures to reduce greenhouse gas emissions in the energy sector, energy efficiency and energy conservation, development of sustainable transport, infrastructure for electric and gas vehicles, smart traffic management systems, sustainable municipal waste management, transition to sustainable land use methods and organic agriculture

Since 2018, an auctioning mechanism for selecting projects of renewable energy sources (hereinafter – RES) has been introduced in Kazakhstan. This mechanism replaced the fixed tariffs that were in effect until 2018, which initially allowed the launch of the renewable energy sector in the Republic of Kazakhstan. hydrogen as well as other alternative sources of energy.

creation of a required infrastructure for EVs in large cities of the country.

Action plan on implementation of the election program of the President of the Republic of Kazakhstan “Just Kazakhstan – for all and everyone, Now and forever” adopted by the Decree of the President of the Republic of Kazakhstan # 2 dated 26 November 2022 contains the following activities that contribute to achieving the NDC target by 2030: to attract by 2029 not less than 150 billion USD worth of direct foreign investment; 60% gasification of the country area; 1,5 times increase of the volume of production using RES;
creation of a required infrastructure for EVs in large cities of the country.

41.3 percent of the population of Kazakhstan lives in rural settlements with poorly developed infrastructure, remote from industrial centers, with a small capacity of the domestic market and with a predominance of energy-intensive export-oriented sectors of the economy, which provide the main revenues of the state budget, and significantly affect economic policy and the exchange rate of the national currency. The Republic of Kazakhstan will need to introduce new and significantly strengthen existing carbon pricing mechanisms in order to achieve its NDC, which has a double dependence on fossil fuels (coal and oil) in the country.

It will also be necessary to increase the share of renewable energy sources (solar and wind) in the balance of electricity production, and to use previously unused capacities to increase the maneuverability of the system. It will be necessary to change the existing dispatching modes of the power grid to more adaptive ones, digitalize the aging energy fleet and introduce the use of digital twins.

The introduction of carbon pricing can lead to an increase in prices for fuel and energy resources and dependent services, and to a significant increase in inflation, which in turn can significantly worsen the welfare of the population.
Lack of access to cheap loans for low-carbon projects, while brown assets have access to guarantees and financing with a potentially lower interest rate.
Lack of consideration of climate criteria and criteria of Sustainable Development Goals in the budgetary process, which leads to risks of financing and potentially stranded assets.

The risk of a shortage of natural gas for decarbonization of energy. Achieving NDC targets implies an increase in natural gas supplies, which requires field development and investment, as well as tariff revisions.

citations.quote: Achievement of NDC targets and carbon neutrality will demand holistic digitalization first of all in the energy sector and the environment to track a carbon footprint and to ensure transparency as well as the creation of an innovation ecosystem both for applied research programs and new financial tools on decarbonization.

Monitoring of the NDC implementation progress will be reported in the Biennial transparency report including the progress of the current plans and programs implementation, policy and practical indicators by using available data of the unified climate platform.

by_document.summary: Reports renewable capacity and generation, and sets renewable-generation, efficiency, heating, fossil-transition and methane objectives or planned measures. It also describes grid resilience and adaptation concerns, plus planned building retrofits, standards and cooling measures.

Sets long-term goals for alternative electricity sources and energy intensity, reports renewable-project auctions as introduced, and describes planned grid, efficiency, building-modernization and gasification measures. changes_between_editions.text: Renewable-electricity goals differ between the editions: KAZ-NDC2 states a 15% renewable share by 2030 and a 50% alternative-source share by 2050; KAZ-NDC1 reports current renewable generation and states goals of 20% renewable-energy development and at least 35% renewable and nuclear generation by 2035, with a conditional clean-energy pathway of 73% by 2035. These figures refer to differently framed targets and are not directly reconciled in the findings.
The energy-intensity targets differ in baseline and horizon: KAZ-NDC2 gives a 50% reduction from 2008 by 2050, while KAZ-NDC1 gives a 20% reduction from 2021 by 2035.

KAZ-NDC1 adds specific methane regulation, leak-reduction and oil-and-gas measures, plus a conditional methane-reduction projection; no specific oil-and-gas methane measure or target was found in KAZ-NDC2’s retrieved evidence.

findings.text: The Environmental Code provides a basis for introducing best available technologies to reduce environmental impacts and improve resource-use efficiency. From 1 January 2025, facilities with a significant negative environmental impact are required to hold a comprehensive environmental permit requiring equipment with the best available techniques; the requirement is stated as forthcoming, not as evidence that equipment has already been installed.

citations.quote: Article 113 of the Code creates a basis for the introduction of the best available technologies aimed at reducing the negative impact on the environment, minimizing and controlling the negative anthropogenic impact on the environment, improving the efficiency of the use of resources that contribute to the transition of the Republic of Kazakhstan to a green economy and low-carbon development. According to Article 418, paragraph 4 of the Code since 1 January 2025, for facilities that have a significant negative impact on the environment, it is mandatory to have a comprehensive environmental permit, which requires the use of equipment with the best available techniques.

A just transition framework is nascent, and practical guidance for reskilling workers, diversifying local economies, and protecting affected households remain limited.
To ensure that no region or community is left behind, the Government will pursue a just transition that:
assessing local labour markets and skills,
supporting re-training and re-deployment of workers,
diversifying regional economies, and
providing social protection for affected households.

It is expected that climate stressors such as increased droughts, changes the river flow regimes and precipitation patterns, increased temperatures, and increased occurrence of extreme weather events are expected to bring agricultural losses to the country, engendering food insecurity in the region by 2050. High soil salinity is already affecting arable lands and impacting crop productivity. Apart from reduced crop yields, rising temperature and changes in rainfall patterns could result in outbreaks of agricultural pests and diseases, including those traveling across national borders.

Feeding sources and grazing areas, particularly pastures, which already face degradation and overgrazing, will be affected by desertification, droughts, and storms. Variability in temperature and precipitation patterns combined with a decrease in water access could contribute to biological stress on animals, affect growth and reproductive patterns, and increase the spread of infectious diseases among livestock.

The impact of climate change on agricultural production disproportionately affects the well-being of different population groups. One of the most vulnerable groups are women living in rural areas, where, along with agricultural work, women traditionally take care of the family and housework.

The general objective of the adaptation chapter of the Environmental Code is to promote the reduction of climate risks in Kazakhstan by building climate resilience while addressing the impacts of climate change, minimizing climate risks, and implementing measures enabling adaptation of natural ecosystems, economic activities, and infrastructure, safeguarding public health, ensuring food security and access to water and gender equality.

Actions already partially undertaken in the agricultural sector include crops diversification, gradual move away from water-intensive crops, shift to water-saving technologies, modernization of drip irrigation and corresponding infrastructure in view of any hypothetical change and redistribution of river runoff in a year, shift to modern organic farming and better soil management to maintain its carbon content, change in fodder for animals to reduce methane emissions from cattle and prevention of overgrazing, responsible management and protection of pastures.
One of the planned measures would be to conduct updated agroclimatic zoning of the territory of the Republic to take into account the observed changes in conditions for the growth of the crops.

Forestry planting programmes will, apart from boosting carbon sequestration on an unprecedented level, support land rehabilitation projects, convert unproductive land to forestry, rejuvenate damaged landscapes and create jobs in the sustainable forestry and timber industry.

Regional problems of neighbouring countries such as the imposition and implementation of sanctions, military conflicts, waves of immigration due to policies, increased prices for food and accommodation, etc. can reduce trade turnover, disrupt the supply chain and weaken the economy of the Republic of Kazakhstan, worsen the social conditions of the population, and accordingly reduce the window for decarbonization.

The Government recognizes that these climate-related challenges demand not only stronger mitigation and adaptation efforts but also dedicated measures to avert, minimize, and address loss and damage (L&D).

Kazakhstan is committed to protecting the most vulnerable populations, including low-income households, women, children, elderly persons, persons with disabilities, and farmers, whose livelihoods are most at risk.

findings.text: Forest cover was reported as low: 12.9 million ha (4.74% of the country); shrubbery and protective plantings covered about 10 million ha, and principal wood species occupied 3.3 million ha. Satellite data showed woodlands covered 1.24% of the country, or 3.48 million ha. Nearly all forests were state-owned and protected, with restrictions on cutting. Felling removed principal wood species from 10 thousand ha per year; saxaul felling and shrub cutting cleared an additional 40 thousand ha per year. Saxaul cutting was prohibited from 2015, and the ban was extended to saxaul trade from 2017.

Current forest cover in Kazakhstan is low: it amounts to 12.9 million ha or 4.74% of the territory. Shrubbery and protective plantings cover about 10 million hectares, while only 3.3 million hectares are occupied by principal wood species: coniferous, soft-wooded, and hard-wooded broadleaved species. Much of the area recognized as forests is not covered by woods, as confirmed by the satellite data, according to which the Kazakhstan woodlands cover just 1.24% of the total country area or 3.48 million hectares. Nearly all forests are state-owned and protected, with restrictions on cutting. Felling of principal wood species removes forest from an area of 10 thousand ha per annum. Felling of saxaul and cutting of shrubbery, registered mainly in the South of Kazakhstan, cleared some additional 40 thousand ha per annum, according to the official statistical data. Since 2015, cutting saxaul is prohibited, and from 2017 this ban was extended to the trade of saxaul.

Kazakhstan pledged to restore at least up to 1.5 million ha of degraded land through afforestation and reforestation until 2030 under the Bonn Challenge. Afforestation of at least up to 1.5 million ha of degraded land under the Bonn Challenge would bring substantial mitigation benefits. Forestry planting programmes will, apart from boosting carbon sequestration on an unprecedented level, support land rehabilitation projects, convert unproductive land to forestry, rejuvenate damaged landscapes and create jobs in the sustainable forestry and timber industry.

Afforestation and reforestation mitigation outcomes under three different scenarios until 2030 were modelled with the use of CBM-CFS3 (Carbon Budget Model of the Canadian Forest Sector) software. In the first three years [after planting] each hectare of coniferous, soft-wooded, or hardwood trees absorbs the average of 1 ton of carbon per year that is equivalent to 3.67 tons of CO2 per year per hectare subject to lack of disturbances. However, later this parameter drops to 0.7 tons of carbon per year per forest hectare. This can be explained by forest aging which is leading to a decrease in carbon dioxide absorption. The 25-year lifespan of commercial forests will provide the country with adaptation benefits (water retention, wood for construction, etc.) as well as increase carbon sinks offsetting anthropogenic emissions that cannot be further mitigated or reduced by other means.

To increase forest cover, the government is planning to improve in the 2022-2030 period the mechanism of support incentivizing the setting up of private industrial plantations and forest nurseries, and implementation of pilot projects in this field supported by public-private partnerships. Further measures are planned to ensure the protection of forests.

In 2020, National Action Plan for the implementation of the Address of the Head of State to the people of Kazakhstan dated September 1, 2020 "Kazakhstan in a new reality: time for action”. It aims to ensure planting of more than 2 billion trees in the forest fund and 15 million in settlements within five years, and it is aligned with the Bonn Challenge goals.

Since 2000, droughts of varying severity have already affected more than 50% of the total land area of Kazakhstan in two out of every five years. The likely consequences include the continued expansion of deserts and arid areas with the possible loss of coastline due to the lowering of the Caspian Sea level.
High soil salinity is already affecting arable lands and impacting crop productivity.
Feeding sources and grazing areas, particularly pastures, which already face degradation and overgrazing, will be affected by desertification, droughts, and storms.

findings.text: Forest cover was reported as low: 12.9 million ha (4.74% of the country); shrubbery and protective plantings covered about 10 million ha, and principal wood species occupied 3.3 million ha. Satellite data showed woodlands covered 1.24% of the country, or 3.48 million ha. Nearly all forests were state-owned and protected, with restrictions on cutting. Felling removed principal wood species from 10 thousand ha per year; saxaul felling and shrub cutting cleared an additional 40 thousand ha per year. Saxaul cutting was prohibited from 2015, and the ban was extended to saxaul trade from 2017.

figures.label: Area occupied by principal wood species
Annual felling of principal wood species

citations.quote: Current forest cover in Kazakhstan is low: it amounts to 12.9 million ha or 4.74% of the territory. Shrubbery and protective plantings cover about 10 million hectares, while only 3.3 million hectares are occupied by principal wood species: coniferous, soft-wooded, and hard-wooded broadleaved species. Much of the area recognized as forests is not covered by woods, as confirmed by the satellite data, according to which the Kazakhstan woodlands cover just 1.24% of the total country area or 3.48 million hectares. Nearly all forests are state-owned and protected, with restrictions on cutting. Felling of principal wood species removes forest from an area of 10 thousand ha per annum. Felling of saxaul and cutting of shrubbery, registered mainly in the South of Kazakhstan, cleared some additional 40 thousand ha per annum, according to the official statistical data. Since 2015, cutting saxaul is prohibited, and from 2017 this ban was extended to the trade of saxaul.

Shrubbery and protective plantings cover about 10 million hectares, while only 3.3 million hectares are occupied by principal wood species: coniferous, soft-wooded, and hard-wooded broadleaved species. Much of the area recognized as forests is not covered by woods, as confirmed by the satellite data, according to which the Kazakhstan woodlands cover just 1.24% of the total country area or 3.48 million hectares. Nearly all forests are state-owned and protected, with restrictions on cutting. Felling of principal wood species removes forest from an area of 10 thousand ha per annum. Felling of saxaul and cutting of shrubbery, registered mainly in the South of Kazakhstan, cleared some additional 40 thousand ha per annum, according to the official statistical data. Since 2015, cutting saxaul is prohibited, and from 2017 this ban was extended to the trade of saxaul.

findings.text: The document reports modeled carbon uptake from afforestation and reforestation under three scenarios through 2030: in the first three years after planting, each hectare of the specified tree types absorbs an average of 1 ton of carbon per year (equivalent, as stated, to 3.67 tons of CO2 per hectare per year), subject to no disturbances; later the stated rate falls to 0.7 tons of carbon per forest hectare per year. It says commercial forests have a 25-year lifespan and describes their expected adaptation benefits and role in increasing carbon sinks. These are modeled outcomes and projections, not achieved removals.

citations.quote: Afforestation and reforestation mitigation outcomes under three different scenarios until 2030 were modelled with the use of CBM-CFS3 (Carbon Budget Model of the Canadian Forest Sector) software. In the first three years [after planting] each hectare of coniferous, soft-wooded, or hardwood trees absorbs the average of 1 ton of carbon per year that is equivalent to 3.67 tons of CO2 per year per hectare subject to lack of disturbances. However, later this parameter drops to 0.7 tons of carbon per year per forest hectare. This can be explained by forest aging which is leading to a decrease in carbon dioxide absorption. The 25-year lifespan of commercial forests will provide the country with adaptation benefits (water retention, wood for construction, etc.) as well as increase carbon sinks offsetting anthropogenic emissions that cannot be further mitigated or reduced by other means.

citations.quote: The 2021-2030 Action Plan contains several measures linked to adaptation to climate change, especially those concerning a reduction in the intensity of the use of water, transformation of agriculture, energy efficiency, modernization of housing and communal services, development of sustainable transport but also conservation of ecosystems and enhancement of forest cover. Several of these measures bring additional benefits to other sectors affected by climate change. For example, afforestation, apart from economic benefits and additional mitigation outcomes, will enable the government to address land erosion, increase water retention and improve groundwater quality.

citations.quote: Current forest cover in Kazakhstan is low: it amounts to 12.9 million ha or 4.74% of the territory. Shrubbery and protective plantings cover about 10 million hectares, while only 3.3 million hectares are occupied by principal wood species: coniferous, soft-wooded, and hard-wooded broadleaved species. Much of the area recognized as forests is not covered by woods, as confirmed by the satellite data, according to which the Kazakhstan woodlands cover just 1.24% of the total country area or 3.48 million hectares. Nearly all forests are state-owned and protected, with restrictions on cutting. Felling of principal wood species removes forest from an area of 10 thousand ha per annum. Felling of saxaul and cutting of shrubbery, registered mainly in the South of Kazakhstan, cleared some additional 40 thousand ha per annum, according to the official statistical data. Since 2015, cutting saxaul is prohibited, and from 2017 this ban was extended to the trade of saxaul.

increase the forestry area till 14,5 million hectares; development of a complex plan for water sector aimed at the conservation of national water ecosystems. Protection of water ecosystems from contamination by the industry;

Kazakhstan pledged to restore at least up to 1.5 million ha of degraded land through afforestation and reforestation until 2030 under the Bonn Challenge. Afforestation of at least up to 1.5 million ha of degraded land under the Bonn Challenge would bring substantial mitigation benefits. Forestry planting programmes will, apart from boosting carbon sequestration on an unprecedented level, support land rehabilitation projects, convert unproductive land to forestry, rejuvenate damaged landscapes and create jobs in the sustainable forestry and timber industry.

Afforestation and reforestation mitigation outcomes under three different scenarios until 2030 were modelled with the use of CBM-CFS3 (Carbon Budget Model of the Canadian Forest Sector) software. In the first three years [after planting] each hectare of coniferous, soft-wooded, or hardwood trees absorbs the average of 1 ton of carbon per year that is equivalent to 3.67 tons of CO2 per year per hectare subject to lack of disturbances. However, later this parameter drops to 0.7 tons of carbon per year per forest hectare. This can be explained by forest aging which is leading to a decrease in carbon dioxide absorption. The 25-year lifespan of commercial forests will provide the country with adaptation benefits (water retention, wood for construction, etc.) as well as increase carbon sinks offsetting anthropogenic emissions that cannot be further mitigated or reduced by other means.

To increase forest cover, the government is planning to improve in the 2022-2030 period the mechanism of support incentivizing the setting up of private industrial plantations and forest nurseries, and implementation of pilot projects in this field supported by public-private partnerships. Further measures are planned to ensure the protection of forests.

In 2020, National Action Plan for the implementation of the Address of the Head of State to the people of Kazakhstan dated September 1, 2020 "Kazakhstan in a new reality: time for action”. It aims to ensure planting of more than 2 billion trees in the forest fund and 15 million in settlements within five years, and it is aligned with the Bonn Challenge goals.

Since 2000, droughts of varying severity have already affected more than 50% of the total land area of Kazakhstan in two out of every five years. The likely consequences include the continued expansion of deserts and arid areas with the possible loss of coastline due to the lowering of the Caspian Sea level.
High soil salinity is already affecting arable lands and impacting crop productivity.
Feeding sources and grazing areas, particularly pastures, which already face degradation and overgrazing, will be affected by desertification, droughts, and storms.
The growing shortage of water, including due to transboundary factors, and the associated degradation of aquatic ecosystems, are among the most pressing problems for Kazakhstan.

The state policy of the Republic of Kazakhstan in the field of adaptation to climate change will also address biodiversity loss, reflecting the principles and goals of the UN Convention on Biological Diversity as well as the UN Convention to Combat Desertification.

changes_between_editions.text: KAZ-NDC2 adds concerns about climate hazards to roads, bridges and buildings, urban heat islands, poorly developed infrastructure in rural settlements, and uncertainty in hydropower potential. These are not repeated in KAZ-NDC1.

Building measures differ in specificity: KAZ-NDC1 sets retrofit-rate and new-building-code targets and describes standards review and metering, while KAZ-NDC2 refers to thermal modernization in its 2021–2030 Action Plan without quantified targets.

KAZ-NDC2 describes city greening and forest belts around major towns; KAZ-NDC1 specifies planned expansion of the green zone around Astana. The editions give different descriptions and do not establish that either measure replaced the other.

Grid measures differ: KAZ-NDC1 describes heat-resilient upgrades and preparation of grids in six oblasts for successive hot days, while KAZ-NDC2 describes adaptive dispatching, digitalization, digital twins and intelligent power-sector systems.

KAZ-NDC1 specifies urban transport-planning measures and emergency protection of critical infrastructure; KAZ-NDC2 mentions sustainable transport in the 2021–2030 Action Plan without specifying network-resilience measures.

changes_between_editions.text: KAZ-NDC2 adds a stated historical drought frequency and concerns about glacier loss, water scarcity and aquatic-ecosystem degradation; these details are not repeated in KAZ-NDC1.
KAZ-NDC1 describes a Water Code legal framework and quantified targets or plans for water quality, irrigation, wastewater treatment and storage. These statements are not repeated in KAZ-NDC2.
